title: NJ Physician Assistant Licensing Act, summarized
body:
Sources:

- **Physician Assistant Licensing Act**, `N.J.S.A. 45:9-27.10 et seq.` (P.L. 1991, c. 378), including `45:9-27.16` scope, `45:9-27.17` physician responsibility, and `45:9-27.19` prescribing and dispensing.
- **N.J.A.C. 13:35-2B**, New Jersey State Board of Medical Examiners rules for physician assistants. Section index and text via the Legal Information Institute, https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-jersey/title-13/chapter-35/subchapter-2B
- Executive Order 415 (January 16, 2026) and Executive Order 13 (February 13, 2026) on the expiration of COVID-era practice waivers, effective **5:00 PM on April 2, 2026**.

This is a summary for someone planning a PA application, not legal advice. Verify against the current rule before relying on any detail.

## Licensure, 13:35-2B.5

- At least `18` years old and of good moral character.
- Graduation from a PA education program accredited by the **Accreditation Review Commission on Education for the Physician Assistant (ARC-PA)**.
- A passing score on the examination administered by the **National Commission on Certification of Physician Assistants (NCCPA)**, that is, the PANCE.
- Holders of a current PA license in another state with substantially equivalent standards may satisfy these requirements without repeating each step.

## Renewal and continuing education, 13:35-2B.7 and 2B.8

- Renewal is **biennial**.
- **`50` continuing education credit hours** per biennial period, in Category I courses approved by the AMA, AAPA, AAFP, AOA or ACCME.
- At least **`1` credit** on prescription opioid drugs: responsible prescribing practices, alternatives to opioids for managing and treating pain, and the risks and signs of opioid abuse, addiction and diversion.
- PAs providing perinatal care must complete **`1` credit** of evidence-based explicit and implicit bias training.
- Up to **`15` credits** earned in the final six months of a period may carry into the next one.

> **Key:** Compare cycles. NJ EMT recertification is `48` hours over `36` months, `24` core and `24` elective. A NJ PA license is `50` Category I credits every `24` months with named required topics.

## Supervision, 13:35-2B.10 and N.J.S.A. 45:9-27.17

New Jersey is a supervision state, not a full-practice-authority state.

- A PA engages in practice **only under the supervision of a physician**, at all times while working in an official capacity.
- Supervision is **continuous but does not require physical presence**, provided the physician and PA maintain contact electronically or by other means.
- The ratio is capped at **`4` PAs per supervising physician**, unless the Board alters it upon application.
- A supervising physician may delegate to physician designees who assume responsibility during an assignment.
- Both parties must ensure the scope of practice is identified, delegated tasks match the PA's competence, physician access is defined, and a performance evaluation process exists.

### The delegation agreement

- A separate **written delegation agreement** with each supervising physician.
- Signed and dated **annually**, updated as the practice or the PA's role changes.
- Kept on file at the practice site, provided to the **Physician Assistant Advisory Committee**, and kept on file by that committee.
- States the PA's role, the authorized practice locations, and **whether the physician requires personal review of all charts and countersignature** of medical services performed, including prescribing and administering medication.

## Scope of practice

A PA may provide any medical service **delegated** by the supervising physician, provided the service:

1. Is within the physician assistant's skills,
2. Forms a component of the supervising physician's scope of practice, and
3. Is provided under physician supervision.

That three-part test is why two NJ PAs in different specialties can have very different day-to-day scopes. Scope follows the supervising physician, not a fixed state list.

## Prescribing, N.J.S.A. 45:9-27.19 and 13:35-2B.12

A PA may order, prescribe, dispense and administer medications and medical devices to the extent delegated. Controlled dangerous substances carry extra conditions:

- The supervising physician must **authorize** the PA to order or prescribe Schedule `II`, `III`, `IV` or `V` CDS.
- The PA must be **registered with the DEA** and hold any other required state and federal authorization, and must **print the DEA registration number** on the order or prescription.
- The statute distinguishes three actions: continuing or reissuing a CDS order the supervising physician wrote; adjusting the dosage of such an order **with prior consultation**; and **initiating** a CDS order for a patient **with prior consultation**.
- The PA must comply with Board regulations and applicable educational and continuing professional education requirements for CDS.

## Currency note

COVID-era executive orders had suspended the statutory supervision and delegation-agreement requirements. **Executive Order 415**, January 16, 2026, terminated those waivers. After a `45-day` extension under **Executive Order 13**, February 13, 2026, they expired at **5:00 PM on April 2, 2026**. New Jersey PAs are again fully subject to the supervision and delegation-agreement requirements.

> **Trap:** Anything published between 2020 and 2025 describing NJ PAs practicing without a delegation agreement is out of date. Check the date on every source before you quote it in an essay or an interview.
